```{r}
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
library(marginaleffects)
library(sf)
library(glmmTMB)

lcflrcv <- read.csv("data/continuitystats_landcover.csv") |>
  filter(crop != "other")
alldf <- read.csv("data/continuitystats_data.csv")
all.mn <- read.csv("data/continuitystats_finaldata.csv")

# function for normalizing within study

z.params.data <-  alldf |> 
  group_by(study) |>
  summarize(
    # stdy.max = max(total.flowers),
    stdy.sd = sd(total.flowers),
    stdy.mn = mean(total.flowers),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

apply.z <- function(x, stdy, z.params = z.params.data){
  study.zprm = dplyr::filter(z.params, study == stdy)
  
  (x - study.zprm$stdy.mn)/study.zprm$stdy.sd
}


```

## Floral resource abundance

I fit a linear regression with a dispersion formula to account for differences in data noisiness between studies. I'm modeling standardized flower counts instead of raw values. I'm not using a gamma distribution model anymore because the data has negative values now.

```{r}

# glm.flrmn4b <- glmmTMB(flr.mn ~ (crop.shandiv + poly(pct.natural,2)) * study, 
#                       dispformula = ~ study,
#                       family = Gamma(link = "log"),
#                       data = all.mn)

glm.flrmn4a <- glmmTMB(flr.mn.zscale ~ crop.shandiv + poly(pct.natural,2) * study, 
                      dispformula = ~ study,
                      data = all.mn)


sjPlot::tab_model(glm.flrmn4a, transform = NULL)

```

### Visualization

```{r}


glm.flrmn.avgpred.nat <- avg_predictions(
  glm.flrmn4a,
  newdata = datagrid(pct.natural = seq(0, 100, by=5), study = unique(all.mn$study)),
  by = c("pct.natural", "study")
)

ggplot(glm.flrmn.avgpred.nat, 
       aes(pct.natural, estimate)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low,
                  ymax = conf.high,
                  fill = study),
              alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(linetype = study, color = study)) +
  geom_point(data = all.mn, 
             mapping = aes(pct.natural, flr.mn.zscale,
                           color = study, 
                           group = study, shape = study),
             inherit.aes = FALSE) + 
  # scale_shape_manual(values = c(12,8,1)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "viridis", direction = -1) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "viridis", direction = -1) +
  egg::theme_article() +
  labs(y="Total flowers (z-score)", x = "% natural area")

```

Here are model-estimated trends and data in their original scales, faceted by study.

```{r}

glm.flrmn.pred.nat <- plot_predictions(
  glm.flrmn4a, 
  condition = list(pct.natural=seq(0,100, by = 5),
                   # crop.shandiv=c(0,1,2),
                   study=unique(all.mn$study)),
  vcov = TRUE, type = "response", draw = FALSE) |> 
  mutate(crop.shandiv = as.numeric(as.character(crop.shandiv)))


ggplot(glm.flrmn.pred.nat, 
       aes(pct.natural, estimate, group = crop.shandiv)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low,
                  ymax = conf.high),
              alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = all.mn, 
             mapping = aes(pct.natural, flr.mn.zscale, color = crop.shandiv, 
                           group = study),
             inherit.aes = FALSE) + 
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "turbo", direction = -1) + 
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "turbo", direction = -1) + 
  egg::theme_article() +
  labs(y="Total flowers", x = "% natural area") +
  facet_wrap(~study, scales = "free_y") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

```

## Floral resource continuity (coefficient of variance)

The best-supported model for floral resource continuity suggests a quadratic response to % natural area and no significant effect of crop diversity.

```{r}

glm.flrcv4a <- glmmTMB(flr.cv ~ crop.shandiv + poly(pct.natural,2) * study, 
                      dispformula = ~ study,
                      data = all.mn)

sjPlot::tab_model(glm.flrcv4a, transform = NULL)

```

### Visualization

The best continuity is achieved at intermediate natural habitat for Iverson and Guezen & Forrest studies. I think this is because intermediate natural habitat landscapes balance the size of the peak bloom against the spread of blooms over time.

```{r}


glm.flrcv2a.pred <- avg_predictions(
  glm.flrcv4a,
  newdata = datagrid(pct.natural = seq(0, 100, by=5), study = unique(all.mn$study)),
  by = c("pct.natural", "study")
)

ggplot(glm.flrcv2a.pred, 
       aes(pct.natural, estimate)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low,
                  ymax = conf.high,
                  fill = study),
              alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(linetype = study, color = study)) +
  geom_point(data = all.mn, 
             mapping = aes(pct.natural, flr.cv,
                           color = study, 
                           group = study, shape = study),
             inherit.aes = FALSE) + 
  # scale_shape_manual(values = c(12,8,1)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "viridis", direction = -1) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "viridis", direction = -1) +
  egg::theme_article() +
  labs(y="Discontinuity (CV)", x = "% natural area")

```

## Flowering peak

I rescaled the main bloom season of each study to 0-1 to compare relative timing of bloom. Peak time is calculated as a weighted mean of the rescaled bloom survey times, using floral counts to weight each period.

The **(new)** best model has interacting terms for % natural area (quadratic) and study. Crop shannon diversity interaction with study is also supported, but not a quadratic term.

```{r}

glm.pktime2d <- glmmTMB(pktime.scale ~ (crop.shandiv + poly(pct.natural,2)) * study, 
                       dispformula = ~ study,
                       data = all.mn)


sjPlot::tab_model(glm.pktime2d, transform = NULL)

```

### Visualization

Peak flowering decreases with naturalness in the landscape but shape of decrease differs between studies. Also, the Hemberger Williams data may not be significant. Will have to post-hoc test these.

```{r}

glm.pktime.pred <- avg_predictions(
  glm.pktime2d,
  newdata = datagrid(pct.natural = seq(0, 100, by=5), study = unique(all.mn$study)),
  by = c("pct.natural", "study")
)

ggplot(glm.pktime.pred, 
       aes(pct.natural, estimate)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low,
                  ymax = conf.high,
                  fill = study),
              alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(linetype = study, color = study)) +
  geom_point(data = all.mn, 
             mapping = aes(pct.natural, pktime.scale,
                           color = study, 
                           group = study, shape = study),
             inherit.aes = FALSE) + 
  # scale_shape_manual(values = c(12,8,1)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "viridis", direction = -1) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "viridis", direction = -1) +
  egg::theme_article() +
  labs(y="Peak flowering time (scaled)", x = "% natural area")


```

Faceted by study. Crop shannon diversity does have a significant effect so I'm showing trends at different crop diversity levels.

```{r}

ggplot(glm.flrpktime.pred.nat,

             inherit.aes = FALSE) +

  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "turbo", direction = -1) + 
  egg::theme_article() +
  labs(y="Peak bloom", x = "% natural area") +
  facet_wrap(~study) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

```

Peak flowering trend by crop diversity. The Guezen & Forrest study has an opposite effect of crop diversity.

## Land cover trends

### Land cover floral count means

Comparison between land cover mean floral counts (over the season) for crop and natural area land covers. Natural land covers are significantly higher in mean floral resources.

```{r}

lcflr.lm0 <- glmmTMB(flr.mn.scale ~ crop + study,
                data = lcflrcv)

lcflr.lm1 <- glmmTMB(flr.mn.scale ~ crop + study, 
                     dispformula = ~study,
                data = lcflrcv)

ggplot(lcflrcv, aes(crop, flr.mn.scale, fill = crop)) + 
  geom_boxplot() +
  # geom_jitter(aes(shape = study), width = 0.2) +
  egg::theme_article() +
  labs(x = "Land cover", y = "Scaled mean flower count") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

lcflr.lm2 <- glmmTMB(flr.mn.scale ~ crop * study,
                     dispformula = ~study,
                     data = lcflrcv)

anova(lcflr.lm1, lcflr.lm2)

sjPlot::tab_model(lcflr.lm1)

```

### Land cover discontinuity

There is not a significant difference in discontinuity between crop and natura land cover types.

```{r}

lccv.lm1 <- lm(flr.cv ~ crop + study, 
                     dispformula = ~study, 
                    data = lcflrcv |> filter(!is.na(flr.cv)))

ggplot(lcflrcv |> filter(!is.na(flr.cv)), aes(crop, flr.cv, fill = crop)) + 
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(aes(shape = study), width = 0.2) +
  egg::theme_article() +
  labs(x = "Land cover", y = "Discontinuity (cv)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

lccv.lm2 <- lm(flr.mn.scale ~ crop * study,
                     dispformula = ~study,
                    data = lcflrcv |> filter(!is.na(flr.cv)))

anova(lccv.lm1, lccv.lm2)

sjPlot::tab_model(lccv.lm1)

```

### Land cover peak times

Bloom peak times of crops are significantly earlier.

```{r}

lcpk.lm1 <- glmmTMB(pktime.scale ~ crop + study, 
                     dispformula = ~study, data = lcflrcv)

ggplot(lcflrcv |> filter(!is.na(flr.cv)), aes(crop, pktime.scale, fill = crop)) + 
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(aes(shape = study), width = 0.2) +
  egg::theme_article() +
  labs(x = "Land cover", y = "Peak flowering time (scaled)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

lcflr.lm2 <- glmmTMB(flr.mn.scale ~ crop * study,
                     dispformula = ~study, data = lcflrcv)

anova(lcflr.lm1, lcflr.lm2)

sjPlot::tab_model(lcpk.lm1)

```
